lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: deciding whether a model is consistent with data
lessonRef.title: Guided practice A: deciding whether a model is consistent with data

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Use this example as the model for the guided set below.

items.prompt: Mean 100, sd 15. What percentage lies between 70 and 130?

steps: That is 100 ± 30, which is two standard deviations.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 53%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±5%, giving 48% to 58%
±53%, giving 0% to 106%
±10%, giving 43% to 63%

items.prompt: In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 42 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 4.2% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 4.2% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 49 and standard deviation 5. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 34 and 64?
choices: about 99.7%
about 50%
about 95%
about 68%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 73%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±73%, giving 0% to 146%
±10%, giving 63% to 83%
±5%, giving 68% to 78%

items.prompt: In 500 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 24 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 4.8% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 4.8% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 166 and standard deviation 6. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 148 and 184?
choices: about 99.7%
about 50%
about 68%
about 95%

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.

items.prompt: A random sample of 100 people gives a sample proportion of 39%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±20%, giving 19% to 59%
±39%, giving 0% to 78%
±1%, giving 38% to 40%
±10%, giving 29% to 49%
